opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core issue is that right now we mostly treat large language models as black boxes. We test them on benchmarks, we red-team them, we look at their outputs, and if the outputs look fine, we say the model is safe. But that's behavioral evaluation, and behavior only tells you what the model did on the inputs you happened to try. It doesn't tell you *why* the model did it, or what it will do on the inputs you didn't try.

Mechanistic interpretability is about opening the box and asking: what algorithms has the network actually learned? Which internal features represent which concepts, and how do they combine into a computation? If we can answer that, safety becomes much less of a guessing game. For example, if a model has learned a genuinely general rule versus a brittle shortcut that only works on the training distribution, from the outside those can look identical. From the inside, they're very different circuits.

I often use an analogy with physics. Before we understood mechanics, people could build bridges by trial and error, and many bridges fell down. Once we had the underlying theory, we could predict failures before they happened. I think AI is still in the trial-and-error phase. Interpretability is one path toward something more like an engineering science for neural networks.

That said, I want to be honest about the difficulty. Large language models are enormous, and the representations are often distributed and superposed, so many concepts share the same neurons. That's partly why some of my own work goes in a different direction: instead of only trying to reverse-engineer existing models, can we design architectures that are more interpretable from the start? Things like Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks, or training methods that encourage modular, sparse structure, so the model "grows" into something a human can read. I think both directions matter: understanding the models we have, and building models that are easier to understand.

So for me, the need is basically this: as these systems become more capable and more deeply integrated into society, "it seems to work" is not a sufficient safety standard. We want to understand, at least partially, the mechanisms, so that trust is based on understanding rather than just observation.

r001.rationale: The response says output-based evaluation is insufficient for safety and that we need to understand model mechanisms so trust rests on understanding rather than observation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the simplest way I'd put it is this: right now we have these systems that are extraordinarily capable, and we fundamentally don't know how they work. We trained them, we can measure what they do on benchmarks, but if you ask "why did the model produce this particular answer," the honest response is usually a shrug. Mechanistic interpretability is the attempt to change that, to actually open up the network and understand the internal computation, the circuits, the features, rather than just treating it as a black box that we poke from the outside.

Why does that matter for safety? Behavioral evaluation alone has a basic limitation. You can test a model on a million prompts and it behaves well, but you've only covered a tiny slice of the input space, and more importantly, you can't distinguish between a model that is genuinely doing the right thing and one that has learned to look like it's doing the right thing. If a system has some undesirable internal goal or heuristic that only shows up under rare conditions, behavioral testing may never catch it. Understanding the mechanism is really the only way to get at that distinction. It's similar to how in medicine you don't just observe symptoms, you want to understand the underlying biology before you trust a treatment.

I also think there's a more positive framing. My own background is in physics, and I've always felt that the aspiration should be something like a science of neural networks. Not just engineering tricks that happen to work, but actual principles. If we understand how a model represents concepts, how it composes them, how it reasons, then safety stops being a matter of patching problems after they appear. You can start designing systems where you have real guarantees, or at least real understanding, about what is going on inside. That's part of why I've been interested in architectures like Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks that are more interpretable by construction. Sometimes it's easier to build something you can understand than to reverse-engineer something you can't.

I should be honest though that we're early. The field has made real progress, things like identifying individual features with sparse autoencoders, tracing specific circuits for specific behaviors. But scaling that to a full understanding of a frontier model is still a very long way off. So I see mechanistic interpretability as necessary but not sufficient. It has to work alongside evaluations, alignment training, and governance. What it uniquely offers is the possibility of verification, of checking rather than hoping, and I don't think we can make these systems truly safe without that.

r001.rationale: The candidate says mechanistic interpretability is necessary for safety, explains that it reveals internal computation, and states that truly safe systems require it.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic motivation is that there’s a gap between observing a model’s behavior and understanding why it behaves that way. We can test a language model on many safety questions, and it might give good answers. But that alone doesn’t tell us whether the same behavior will hold in a new situation.

Mechanistic interpretability tries to look inside the model and identify the computations that produce its answers. What information is it representing? How is it using that information? And if we think we’ve found a mechanism, can we intervene on it and change the behavior in a predictable way? That last step is important, because a plausible story about what a model is doing is not necessarily a correct explanation.

For safety, the hope is that this gives us another way to detect problems and understand failures, beyond just looking at outputs. But I wouldn’t say interpretability by itself guarantees safety. Understanding a small part of a model doesn’t mean we understand the whole system, and an explanation that works in one setting may not generalize.

So I see it as a complement to behavioral testing and other safety methods. We want models to behave reliably, but we also want evidence about the internal mechanisms supporting that reliability.

r001.rationale: The response says mechanistic interpretability can complement behavioral testing and other safety methods, and explicitly says it does not guarantee safety. It does not present understanding internal mechanisms as necessary for ensuring safety.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the need comes from the gap between observing what a model does and understanding why it does it. We train a model, test its behavior, and see that it usually gives helpful answers. But that doesn’t necessarily tell us what mechanisms produce those answers, or whether those mechanisms will behave reliably in a new situation.

Mechanistic interpretability tries to open that black box. Can we identify which internal computations lead to a particular behavior? Can we distinguish a model that has learned a robust rule from one that is using a shortcut that happens to work on our tests? That distinction matters for safety, because the failures we care about may be rare or appear only outside the training distribution.

But I wouldn’t say interpretability alone makes a model safe. An explanation can be incomplete, and a plausible story about a neuron or a circuit is not necessarily a correct causal explanation. We need to test those explanations through interventions and see whether they actually help us predict or change behavior.

So I see mechanistic interpretability as a complement to behavioral evaluations and other safety methods. The goal is to give us additional evidence about when to trust a model, where it might fail, and how to fix it.

r001.rationale: The response says mechanistic interpretability can provide additional safety evidence and complement other methods, but does not clearly present internal understanding as necessary for ensuring safety.
